canonicalCards.recommendedFirstExperiment: Copy one phrase and apply the same ride once as pre-insert region/Gain automation and once as fader automation, then compare processor response.
stopOrUndo: Stop once you can repeatably hear whether the ride should change compression/saturation or only the audible balance in the full context. Back off or undo if Moving gain upstream can alter tone and detector behavior; moving it downstream may leave the processor reacting badly.

canonicalCards.question: What should I understand about dynamic range and Loudness Range, and why does it matter?
canonicalCards.rationale: Dynamic range has multiple meanings. LRA describes statistical loudness variation across suitable programme material; it is not a universal punch score or a meaningful metric for every short clip.
canonicalCards.recommendedFirstExperiment: Measure a full representative programme with Loudness Meter, then compare local transient behavior separately rather than using LRA alone.
stopOrUndo: Stop once you can repeatably hear section-to-section loudness variation alongside local transient impact in the full context. Back off or undo if Treating LRA as a fixed delivery target can encourage unnecessary compression or misleading short-clip readings.
Reset the meter and restore original dynamics processing.

canonicalCards.directCandidateAnswer: A loud master can still translate poorly because loudness, tonal balance, transient shape, stereo image, codec behavior, and playback gain interact. Diagnose the specific failure instead of adding gain. The result—the master measures correctly but still feels smaller—suggests the direction may be useful but the amount, stage, or scope needs refinement rather than a complete restart.
evidenceNeeded: The exact source, bus, output, plug-in order, meter position, and current Logic version.
A matched before/after comparison using the same representative musical section.
Input, output, gain-reduction, peak, true-peak, RMS/LUFS, and routing evidence only where relevant.
The user’s report of what became cleaner, louder, denser, flatter, harsher, punchier, quieter, or more cohesive.

myths.correction: -18 dBFS is sometimes used as an average/reference orientation, not a universal peak target.
myths.myth: Every track should peak at exactly -18 dBFS.

myths.correction: Waveform size is not sound quality; clipped capture cannot be repaired by turning down later.
myths.myth: The waveform must be large to sound professional.

myths.correction: Modern 24-bit capture allows generous headroom without sacrificing practical quality.
myths.myth: 24-bit recording needs peaks near 0 dBFS.

myths.correction: The fader may be after inserts and may not change processor input.
myths.myth: A lower fader fixes overdriven plug-ins upstream.

myths.correction: Calibration and headroom behavior are product-specific.
myths.myth: All analog-model plug-ins are calibrated to exactly -18 dBFS.

myths.correction: Converters, nonlinear plug-ins, fixed stages, buses, and physical outputs still have limits or level-dependent behavior.
myths.myth: Floating point means gain staging never matters.

myths.correction: A red internal meter may be a warning in a floating-point stage, but the exact stage matters.
myths.myth: Red on any internal channel means the file is destroyed.

myths.correction: It only changes a later stage and may conceal upstream overload.
myths.myth: Turning down the master fader repairs clipping everywhere.

myths.correction: Auto-gain behavior may be approximate and program-dependent.
myths.myth: Auto Gain always makes fair A/B comparisons.

myths.correction: They are accurate for a different point in the chain.
myths.myth: Pre-fader meters are always more accurate.

myths.correction: Normalization can erase useful relationships and alter nonlinear processor input.
myths.myth: Normalize every file before mixing.

myths.correction: It also controls nonlinear response, detector behavior, noise, sends, and fader usability.
myths.myth: Gain staging is only about avoiding clipping.

myths.correction: Within practical 24-bit/floating workflows, moderate digital attenuation is recoverable.
myths.myth: A quiet digital track has permanently lost detail.

myths.correction: Monitor level normally changes playback loudness, not file level.
myths.myth: The monitor knob changes the mix signal.

myths.correction: Run one reversible, level-matched comparison of one candidate variable; listen in context for the named improvement, stop if a preservation goal worsens, then undo to the saved state.
myths.myth: A bus and an aux are two unrelated things in Logic.

myths.correction: A send normally creates a parallel feed while the dry path continues.
myths.myth: A send creates a subgroup.

myths.correction: Folder and Summing Stacks have different signal-flow behavior.
myths.myth: Folder Stack processing affects all subtracks like a Summing Stack.

myths.correction: Shared compression is useful only if its gain movement supports the music.
myths.myth: Every group needs compression for glue.

myths.correction: It can also blur attacks, add harshness, and reduce separation.
myths.myth: Bus saturation always makes tracks feel like one thing.

myths.correction: Bus EQ changes every member, including those not causing the problem.
myths.myth: Bus EQ is always more musical than source EQ.

myths.correction: A VCA controls members; an aux receives and processes summed audio.
myths.myth: VCA and aux faders do the same thing.

myths.correction: Parallel paths add processed energy and can still reduce contrast or cause phase problems.
myths.myth: Parallel compression preserves dynamics automatically.

myths.correction: Unity is convenient but not a law; stage placement and automation matter.
myths.myth: The bus fader should always stay at 0 dB.

myths.correction: Deep routing can obscure gain, latency, and ownership.
myths.myth: Nested buses are always more professional.

myths.correction: Rooms, parallel paths, samples, or special effects may need different routing.
myths.myth: All drums belong on the same bus.

myths.correction: Lead and support roles may require separate control.
myths.myth: All vocals should share one bus chain.

myths.correction: Useful gain reduction is program- and goal-dependent.
myths.myth: A bus compressor should show a fixed amount of gain reduction.

myths.correction: Solo hides masking, hierarchy, and total loudness.
myths.myth: If the bus sounds better solo, it is better in the mix.

myths.correction: Peak measures instantaneous extrema; perceived loudness depends on energy and weighting over time.
myths.myth: Peak level tells you perceived loudness.

myths.correction: LUFS does not replace peak/true-peak control.
myths.myth: LUFS prevents clipping.

myths.correction: They use different weighting, gating, and standards.
myths.myth: RMS and LUFS are identical.

myths.correction: Integrated loudness depends on the measured programme range.
myths.myth: Integrated LUFS from a chorus loop represents the full song.

myths.correction: LRA describes macro loudness variation and is unreliable for some short content.
myths.myth: LRA is a punch meter.

myths.correction: Inter-sample/true peaks may exceed sample peaks.
myths.myth: 0 dBFS sample peaks guarantee no clipping after conversion.

myths.correction: Limiting changes peaks, envelope, distortion, and often stereo behavior.
myths.myth: A limiter makes audio loud without changing it.

myths.correction: It cannot reconstruct clipped input samples.
myths.myth: A limiter repairs clipped recordings.

myths.correction: True-peak and encoding behavior may require margin.
myths.myth: A limiter ceiling of 0 dB is always safest.

myths.correction: It still changes waveform and harmonics.
myths.myth: Soft clipping is transparent.

myths.correction: Small controlled clipping can be a deliberate peak-control choice.
myths.myth: Hard clipping is always unusable.

myths.correction: Excess limiting can remove transient contrast and make normalized playback smaller.
myths.myth: More LUFS always sounds more powerful.

myths.correction: Playback normalization targets are not universal mastering mandates.
myths.myth: Streaming services require masters at exactly -14 LUFS.

myths.correction: It is an estimate of playback gain adjustment.
myths.myth: A loudness penalty is a quality score.

myths.correction: It depends on window, source, and arrangement.
myths.myth: Crest factor alone measures dynamic quality.

myths.correction: Arrangement and intent differ.
myths.myth: Dynamic range should be the same in every genre.

myths.correction: It can alter sound and may be unnecessary in some private/internal contexts.
myths.myth: True-peak limiting should always be on.

myths.correction: It redistributes peak-control artifacts.
myths.myth: Clipping before limiting creates free loudness.

myths.correction: Multiple stages can help or accumulate damage.
myths.myth: Several limiters are automatically cleaner than one.

myths.correction: Source envelope, note balance, arrangement, or detector filtering may be the real cause.
myths.myth: Low-end limiter pumping is solved only by faster release.

myths.correction: It can obscure transient and balance decisions.
myths.myth: A master bus limiter should hide unfinished balance problems.

myths.correction: There is no universal requirement when the file is unclipped and processing is documented.
myths.myth: Mastering needs exactly -6 dBFS peak headroom.

myths.correction: True peak estimates reconstructed waveform maxima between samples.
myths.myth: True peak and sample peak are the same thing.

myths.correction: They represent different time windows.
myths.myth: Momentary, short-term, and integrated loudness are interchangeable.

myths.correction: Album relationships may be intentionally varied.
myths.myth: The loudest section alone defines album loudness intent.

myths.correction: Monitoring level changes perception, not file meter readings.
myths.myth: Turning up monitoring makes the master measure louder.

myths.correction: Intermediate nonlinear or fixed stages may already distort.
myths.myth: If the final meter is safe, every earlier stage is safe.

myths.correction: Tonal balance, transients, width, codecs, and arrangement still matter.
myths.myth: If the mix meets LUFS and true peak targets, it will translate.
